title: Legionella and water safety awareness
siteNotes: The venue's legionella risk assessment, who the responsible person is, and who carries out water checks (your manager will show you).
The flushing schedule: which outlets, rooms and showers, how often, and how it is recorded.
Which rooms and outlets are little used or likely to sit empty (for example seasonal or event rooms).
The shower head and hose cleaning and descaling schedule, and who does it.
How and to whom to report dirty, stagnant, smelly or tepid water, and what happens next.
Where the water temperature checks and records are kept by the maintenance team.
Who in this venue actually takes the water temperature readings and keeps the records (the session says 'usually the maintenance team').
legalNotes: Duty to assess and control the risk of legionella: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, COSHH 2002 and the HSE Approved Code of Practice L8, with detailed advice in HSG274 (https://www.hse.gov.uk/legionnaires/). The overview page confirmed this duty sits with employers and those in control of premises.

Growth range 20 to 45 degrees C, dormant below 20, not surviving above 60: stated on HSE's page on managing legionella in hot and cold water systems (https://www.hse.gov.uk/healthservices/legionella.htm). Verified in a summary of that page. That page is written for health services, but the temperature facts apply generally.

Flush infrequently used outlets, including showerheads and taps, at least weekly: same HSE page; HSE's landlord guidance also says outlets should be used at least once a week (https://www.hse.gov.uk/legionnaires/legionella-landlords-responsibilities.htm). Verified. The venue's own risk assessment sets the actual schedule.

Shower heads and hoses: HSE's healthcare page says clean and de-scale at least quarterly. Because that page is for health services, the slides say only 'as scheduled by your risk assessment'. The landlord page says showers need regular cleaning and disinfection.

Temperature checks and records: HSE lists routine checks such as monthly hot and cold distribution temperatures at sentinel outlets (healthcare page). Not taught as a staff task; maintenance carry it out per the venue's assessment.

Symptoms: Legionnaires' disease is a form of pneumonia; early symptoms can look like flu. Search summaries listed fever, cough, muscle aches, headaches and shortness of breath, usually 2 to 14 days after exposure. This session says only 'flu-like illness, cough, fever, shortness of breath'. The HSE symptoms page was not read directly. Not a diagnosis tool.

NOT VERIFIED: the HSE page naming what a housekeeper must personally do. Running taps and showers before guest arrival is good practice following the flushing advice; the venue's risk assessment must confirm it.

Review 6 Oct 2026: ACOP L8 (4th edition, 2013) is still the current code; HSG274 is the technical guidance (Part 2 for hot and cold water). Re-confirmed in secondary summaries of HSG274 Part 2: infrequently used outlets flushed at least weekly; shower heads and hoses cleaned and descaled at least quarterly; legionella grows roughly 20 to 45C, is dormant below 20C and killed at 60C and above. The HSE pages themselves were not all re-read. Change: who does the temperature checks is a venue matter, so slide 5 and its check now say 'usually' and 'normally', and it is added to siteNotes. Also 'a bacteria' corrected to 'bacteria live'.

cards.title: Legionella and water safety awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why still, warm water is a risk
- flush and run outlets as your manager has shown you
- spot and report water that is not right

cards.title: A real risk in still water
cards.body:
Legionella bacteria live in water. It can cause Legionnaires' disease, a serious and sometimes fatal form of pneumonia, caught by breathing in tiny droplets, for example from a shower.

> Guests, staff and anyone who showers or uses taps can be affected. Older people and those with health conditions are more at risk.

items.label: Legionella can multiply in this range
Legionella does not survive above this

cards.title: Warm, still and dirty is the problem
cards.body:
Legionella grows when water is warm and stays still, with scale, rust or slime to feed on. A quiet room, a seldom-used tap or a spare shower can all be a problem.

The aim is simple: keep hot water hot, cold water cold and keep it moving.

items.title: Dirty
items.text: Scale, rust and slime give food.

cards.title: Flush and run the water
cards.body:
Unused outlets should be flushed at least weekly. Before a guest arrives in a room that has been empty, run the taps and showers as your manager has shown you.

**Your manager will show you** the flushing schedule and how to record it.

items.title: Check the list
items.text: Know which rooms and outlets are due.

items.title: Run it
items.text: Run taps and showers in the way you were shown.

items.title: Look and smell
items.text: Is it clear, clean and the right temperature?

cards.title: Showers make the droplets
cards.body:
A shower makes a fine spray that can be breathed in, so shower heads and hoses need regular cleaning, descaling and disinfecting to the schedule.

Only do this if you have been trained. **Your manager will show you** the schedule and the method.

left.title: Do
items: Report limescale or slime on heads

right.title: Do not
items: Skip a room because it looks clean
Leave a shower unused for weeks

cards.title: Everyone has a part
cards.body:
Water temperature checks and records are done by a named person, usually the maintenance team. Housekeeping and others run outlets, notice problems and report them. There is a risk assessment and a responsible person.

**Your manager will show you** who they are.

items.title: Maintenance
items.text: Temperature checks, records and scheduled cleaning.

items.title: Responsible person
items.text: Oversees the risk assessment and plan.

cards.title: If it looks or feels wrong, say so
cards.body:
Report water that is dirty, cloudy, smelly, slow to run hot or only ever tepid. Tell your supervisor or maintenance, and keep guests out of that room if told to.

Also know the symptoms: flu-like illness, fever, cough or shortness of breath. If you or a guest feel unwell and think it could be linked, tell your manager and seek medical advice.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Legionella grows in warm, still water, roughly 20 to 45°C
- Flush little-used outlets at least weekly and run water before arrival
- Showers need scheduled cleaning, so do not skip it
- Report dirty, stagnant or tepid water straight away
- Only do what you have been trained to do

cards.q: A room has been empty for two weeks and a guest arrives this afternoon. What should happen?
options: Nothing, the water will be fine
Run the taps and shower as shown, then record it
Spray some disinfectant on the shower head
Turn the room heating up for the guest
cards.why: Water that sits still can become a risk. Running outlets before arrival, as shown, helps keep it moving.

cards.q: Legionella grows best in warm water that has been left standing.
cards.why: Warm, still water, roughly 20 to 45°C, with scale or slime, is where it multiplies.

cards.q: At least how often should a little-used tap or shower be flushed?
options: Once a month
Once a year
At least weekly
Only when a guest complains
cards.why: HSE guidance says infrequently used outlets should be flushed at least weekly.

options: A shower that runs clear and hot
Water that smells or looks cloudy
A tap that has been used daily
Hot water that only ever runs tepid
A guest asking for extra towels
cards.why: Smelly, cloudy or tepid water can point to a problem and should be reported to maintenance or your supervisor.

cards.q: A colleague has a cough and fever after working in a very quiet wing and wonders about the water. What is best?
options: Tell them to ignore it
Tell your manager and suggest medical advice
Tell them it is Legionnaires' disease
Warn all the guests in that wing
cards.why: Symptoms can look like flu. Do not diagnose. Tell a manager so it can be looked at, and the colleague should get medical advice.

cards.q: Which water is most at risk of legionella growth?
options: Hot water kept above 60°C
Cold water that stays cold and flowing
Warm water sitting unused for weeks
Water from a tap used every day
cards.why: Warm, still water, roughly 20 to 45°C, is where it grows.

cards.q: Shower heads only need cleaning if a guest complains.
cards.why: Shower heads and hoses are cleaned and descaled on a schedule, whether or not anyone complains.

cards.q: Who normally carries out the water temperature checks and keeps the records?
options: Guests
The maintenance team
Whoever is nearest
The laundry team
cards.why: Maintenance normally carry out temperature checks and keep the records, as set out in the venue's plan. Your manager will show you who.

cards.q: You can catch Legionnaires' disease by breathing in tiny droplets, such as shower spray.
cards.why: It is caught by inhaling droplets of contaminated water. It is not passed from person to person in the usual way.

cards.q: You see limescale and slime on a shower head while cleaning a room. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, as guests rarely look
Report it so it is cleaned and descaled
Hide it with a new shower curtain
Rinse it with cold water only
cards.why: Scale and slime feed bacteria. Report it so it is cleaned as scheduled.
